name: Carijona

new_statements.rule_in_words: No published rule for the position of word stress in Carijona was found. The only first-hand remark (Koch-Grunberg 1908, Hianakoto-Umaua dialect) says word stress shifts between citation form and sentence context without saying where it falls; the only modern comparative treatment (Meira 1998) explicitly declines to state anything because the sources' stress marks (Koch-Grunberg 1908, Huber & Reed 1992) disagree and Robayo does not mark stress. The sister languages Tiriyo and Akuriyo have iambic rhythmic stress (Meira 1998:18), but Meira does not extend this to Karihona.
new_statements.domain_note: Koch-Grunberg's remark contrasts isolation (citation) forms with sentence context, implying phrase-level effects on word accent; no word-level rule given.
new_statements.identity_note: Koch-Grunberg 1908 describes the Hianakoto-Umaua of the Macaya/Cunyary (upper Apaporis), which he and later authors (Durbin & Seijas 1973; Meira 1998:7) treat as a dialect of the same language as Carijona/Guaque; Glottolog files it under cari1279. Meira 1998 uses the spelling Karihona; Guerrero-Beltran uses Karijona (Puerto Nare, Guaviare). All refer to cari1279.

new_statements.quote: Les phonèmes / ï / et / e / se réalisent [ ϖ ] et [ √ ], ils acquièrent un trait de postériorité à la suite de consonnes vélaires. L'accent vient sur la pénultième syllabe du mot.
new_statements.translation: The phonemes /ï/ and /e/ are realised [ɨ] and [ʌ]; they acquire a back feature after velar consonants. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word.
new_statements.citation: Robayo, Camilo. 1989. "En faisant une rame": texte carijona. Amerindia 14. Paris: Association d'Ethnolinguistique Amerindienne.

L'accent vient sur la pénultième syllabe du mot." — identical to the compiler quote (the text's "[ √ ]" is a font artefact; the 300-dpi render shows "[ ʌ ]", so the compiler translation [ɨ]/[ʌ] is right). A a full-text search for stress/accent all 14 pages for accent/pénulti/syllabe/tonique/prosod hits only these two lines (116-117), so it is the sole stress statement in the work. The sentence is an unconditioned penultimate rule with no weight, secondary-stress or exception clause…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penultimate: penultimate stress) and as the existing statement's reading 'fixed: penultimate syllable'. It is the only first-hand explicit stress rule for Carijona found so far; it supersedes Meira 1998's 'nothing can be said here about stress in Karihona', which did not use this source.3 mentions accent/pénultième/syllabe).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is on the penultimate syllable; a one-sentence statement with no conditions, no weight reference, no exceptions.
new_statements.exceptions: none mentioned; the Carijona forms in the text and glosses carry no stress marks (all acute/grave marks in the PDF text are French orthography), so the statement cannot be checked against the data in the same work
new_statements.identity_note: Robayo 1989 describes the Carijona spoken near Miraflores (Comisaria del Guaviare, Colombia), from a text recorded in Bogota in 1986 with the speaker Horacio Carijona 'Nigua' (d. 1987); no dialect split is stated. Huber & Reed 1992 (not opened) would cover the Carijona (cbd) column of a comparative wordlist.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog records fixed penultimate stress (Robayo 1989: 'L'accent vient sur la pénultième syllabe du mot'). Huber & Reed 1992 states no rule, but its phonetic CJ transcriptions place the stress stroke on the final syllable in about two thirds of the sampled forms and on the penult in the remaining third, which at face value is not a fixed-penultimate pattern. Meira 1998:19 (already in existing_statements) had judged exactly this source (his Kh2) 'inconsistent and frequently in disagreement' with Koch-Grunberg and declined to use it; my sample confirms the inconsistency. The lexibank 'hubercolumbian' digitisation used in earlier passes dropped these strokes (1 acute in 366 rows), which is…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated. The book is a 375-item comparative wordlist; the Carijona (CJ) row is explicitly phonetic IPA and nearly every CJ form carries the IPA primary-stress stroke (placed before the stressed syllable, the book's convention as shown by Tucanoan forms like jẽˈbẽ́-rõ where the acute follows the stroke). Reading items 1-92 by eye (84 non-blank first forms): the last stroke precedes the FINAL syllable in 58 forms (iiniˈko, iidaˈrɯ, emeʒaˈrɯ, tuˈna, maˈma, haˈha, karihoˈna, kanaˈwa, kadeˈro..) and the PENULTIMATE in 26 (iˈdʒeri, ooˈnari, eeˈnuru, iwaˈkuru, ˈhuhu, ˈgɯri, ˈiiba, ekajaˈkari, iˈwasa..); none antepenultimate. Even disyllables split (ˈhutu, ˈhuhu, ˈgɯri vs tuˈna, maˈma, βeˈβe). So the primary transcriptions show word stress on one of the last two syllables, most often the final one in citation form, with no consistent single position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Longer forms often carry two or more strokes (ˈʒamaraˈtari, aˈhɯritʃikaˈrɯ, ˈsamarakaˈtɯ, ˈmanaˈmanakaˈne, jaˈnuroˈhɯrɯˈtɯhɯ), i.e. additional (secondary or rhythmic) stresses are transcribed, frequently one on the first or second syllable plus one at the right edge; the book does not label primary vs secondary.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated (no prose on Carijona stress). The only stress note in the apparatus concerns another language: 'WM Acento no se ha indicado (stress has not been marked)' (Waunana). Doubled initial vowels (iiniˈko, ooˈnari, eeˈnuru) are phonetic length, not stress marks.
new_statements.identity_note: Huber & Reed's CJ column is Carijona of the upper Vaupes, Yari and lower Caqueta rivers (110 speakers, p.17), data from SIL members Roger Van Otterloo & James Peckham; Robayo 1989's statement is for the Carijona of Miraflores (Guaviare), speaker of the Hianakoto clan from La Pedrera. Same language (cari1279); no dialect split is claimed by either source.

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction between statements of placement, because only one source states a placement: Robayo 1989 (fieldworker, first-hand) gives penultimate word stress without qualification. The tension is one of confidence: Meira 1998 (pp.18-19, 57, already held by the project) declined to say anything about Karihona stress because Robayo's 1986/1987 manuscripts do not mark stress and the stress marks in Huber & Reed 1992 and Koch-Grunberg 1908 are inconsistent and disagree, and Koch-Grunberg 1908 (p.955) noted that the stress of a word often differs between isolation and sentence context. The catalog's penultimate rule therefore rests on Robayo 1989's single sentence. Robayo 1989 (first-hand linguist, Amerindia 14, p.3) states penultimate word stress, and that is the catalog's record. Huber & Reed 1992 gives no rule but its phonetic IPA transcriptions of Carijona (Van Otterloo & Peckham, SIL) mark stress mostly on the final syllable (58 of 84 sampled items 1-92) and otherwise on the penult (26), never earlier; Meira 1998:19 already called these marks inconsistent and in disagreement with Koch-Grunberg 1908, whose own remark (p.955) is that a word's stress differs in isolation vs in a sentence. So the wordlist evidence is in tension with a strict fixed: penultimate syllable rule (it suggests right-edge stress heard variably as final or penultimate in citation forms), but it is not a competing rule statement; the explicit statement (Robayo) remains the best-supported readin…
